items.followUp: Define respiration and write its balanced equation.

rubric.why: The definition should identify photosynthesis as the light-driven process by which plants make food.
rubric.description: Defines photosynthesis as the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential idea that green plants use light energy to make glucose. Accept equivalent wording that includes chlorophyll.

rubric.why: The equation must show the reactants and products in the correct balanced proportions.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation, with carbon dioxide and water as reactants and glucose and oxygen as products.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy, in the presence of chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.

items.followUp: Give one example each of an intracellular and an extracellular enzyme.

rubric.why: The key distinction is where an intracellular enzyme acts.
rubric.description: States that intracellular enzymes act inside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their site of action as inside the cell.

rubric.why: Extracellular enzymes are released to act outside the cells that produce them.
rubric.description: States that extracellular enzymes are secreted and act outside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying secretion or action outside the cell.

modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes are produced and act inside the cells in which they are made.
Extracellular enzymes are produced by cells and secreted to act outside those cells.

items.followUp: Describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.

rubric.why: The suitable model is identified by name.
rubric.description: Names the induced-fit model of enzyme action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the induced-fit model.

rubric.why: The model explains substrate binding through a flexible active site that changes shape to fit the substrate.
rubric.description: Explains that the active site changes shape when the substrate binds, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the active-site shape change and fit with the substrate.

modelAnswer: The induced-fit model is the suitable model of enzyme action.
The enzyme's active site is flexible; when a substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.

items.followUp: Name the two vascular tissues in plants and state what each transports.

rubric.why: The plant vascular system consists of its conducting tissues, xylem and phloem.
rubric.description: Identifies xylem and phloem as the vascular tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both xylem and phloem.

rubric.why: The vascular system conducts materials through the plant.
rubric.description: Defines the vascular system as the system that transports materials throughout a plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it conducts or transports substances through the plant.

modelAnswer: The vascular system is the system of conducting tissues that transports materials throughout a plant.
It consists of xylem and phloem.

items.followUp: Explain how water and minerals are transported from the roots to the leaves of a plant.

rubric.why: Food transport in plants occurs through the phloem and is called translocation.
rubric.description: Identifies phloem as the tissue that transports food in plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem as the food-conducting tissue or identifying the process as translocation.

rubric.why: Loading sucrose into sieve tubes is a key step in food translocation.
rubric.description: States that sucrose is loaded into the phloem sieve tubes, with the help of companion cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing sucrose loading into the sieve tubes.

rubric.why: Water enters the phloem by osmosis and increases pressure in the sap.
rubric.description: Explains that water enters the phloem by osmosis, increasing pressure in the phloem sap.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the water-by-osmosis step and its pressure effect.

rubric.why: A pressure difference moves phloem sap from the source toward the sink.
rubric.description: States that pressure drives sap from a high-pressure source toward a lower-pressure sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining pressure-driven movement from source to sink.

rubric.why: Food is unloaded at sinks for use or storage.
rubric.description: States that food is unloaded at sinks, where it is used or stored.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying food unloading at sinks for use or storage.

modelAnswer: Food made in leaves is transported to other parts of the plant through the phloem; this movement is called translocation.
At a source, sucrose is loaded into the phloem sieve tubes, with the help of companion cells.
Water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis, increasing pressure in the phloem sap.
The pressure difference drives the sap from the source, where pressure is high, toward sinks, where pressure is lower.
At sinks, food is unloaded and used or stored; water can return to the xylem.
